newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai leads clean up of China state sector.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai leads clean up of China state sector.

text.p: Shanghai is leading the way for China's bankrupt, inefficient state enterprise sector, closing down and merging firms at a faster rate than any other part of the country, city officials and analysts said.

State-owned firms still dominate China's economy, accounting for 48 percent of industrial output and 30 percent of urban employment. But thanks to decades of mis-management and protection from market forces, about half lose money.
Shanghai, China's largest and most productive city, has been told to get on with solving the state enterprise problem, which is weighing on national finances and threatening social stability.

"Shanghai will lead the whole country and be the first to create a modern enterprise system in three years," Xu Jianguo, deputy director of the Shanghai Economic Commission, told reporters in a briefing.
Shanghai had merged 700 enterprises and let 58 firms go bankrupt since 1994, officials said. The city planned another 100 mergers and 50 bankruptcies in 1997, they said.

The city's top 250 state firms, accounting for 80 percent of the city's state assets and one-third of its workers, have also been told to operate on purely commercial terms, ending the loan hand-outs which keep many of the other enterprises afloat.

"Shanghai has done better than the rest of the country because it's a trial site," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "The central government has done more to force Shanghai to pursue reforms.
"But it's just starting and we don't know how well the reforms will function."

Shanghai's 1,500 state enterprises had lowered their average debt-to-asset ratio to 67.1 percent in 1996, while the current national average was 80 percent, said Huang Qifan, deputy secretary general of the Shanghai city government. Slashing away at the state sector in Shanghai has had a heavy toll in employment terms -- one million workers have been laid off from state firms since 1990, though many have found new jobs.
According to official figures, the unemployment rate in Shanghai has been kept at 2.8 percent thanks to active re-employment programmes.

Shanghai was the first in 1996 to set up large scale re-employment centres to help workers laid off from the textile and instrument industries to receive training and find new jobs, said Ye Mingzhong, deputy director of the Shanghai Labour Bureau.
The two centres found jobs for 58,000 of 115,000 registered laid off workers last year, and more such centres would be opened this year to help workers in other industrial sectors, Ye said.

Shanghai officials said the acceleration of the reforms had been made possible by a breakthrough in creating a city system of unemployment benefits, old age pensions and medical care costs to a large extent independent of the state enterprises.
Under the schemes, the cost of social services was split between the state enterprises, the government and society instead of being borne by the state firms alone, they said.
But a question mark remains over state enterprises' bad debts, which are basically unrecoverable by the banks who hold them, analysts say.
Officials declined to give figures for the debts of Shanghai's state enteprises, except to say that the 100 firms expected to go bankrupt in 1997 had debts of six billion yuan ($723 million).
